newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Megawati seen cast to sidelines.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Megawati seen cast to sidelines.

text.p: Indonesia's main opposition figure is expected to be sidelined this week as lists of candidates for next year's parliamentary elections are finalised with her name conspicuous by its absence, analysts said.

The government no longer recognises Megawati Sukarnoputri as an official of the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) she once led and she has refused to accept any offer of compromise with a government-backed party rival.
Megawati is the chief symbol of dissent against President Suharto's government.
Indonesia's three recognised political parties, including the PDI, must submit their lists of candidates for the elections on Monday.

Dropping her from the PDI list would be the culmination of a four-month campaign by the government to stifle Megawati's growing popularity and ensure she does not pose a threat to the ruling Golkar party, analysts and diplomats said.
Megawati, daughter of late founding president Sukarno, has faced near continuous pressure since June when she was ousted from the PDI leadership by the government-backed faction.
Last week, the military said Megawati and her supporters had no right to conduct political activities and that their inauguration of a new party headquarters was unacceptable.

On Saturday, immigration officials at Jakarta's international airport initially prevented her from leaving on a weekend trip to Singapore but she was later allowed to travel after insisting on being shown written instructions banning her from leaving the country.
There appears little Megawati can do in response except to continue her campaign for political rehabilitation, analysts said.

"The arena of fighting now is not to get the formal position in parliament, which she knows she is not getting, but basically to expose that this is unfair and it is not legitimate," said political commentator Arief Budiman.
Golkar, PDI and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) are the only three political entities permitted by the government to contest parliamentary elections.
Megawati has said her ousting is illegal and is challenging it in court but the government has said it no longer recognises her as a political leader.

Her supporters and other activists held almost daily protest rallies at the PDI headquarters in Jakarta after the ousting. On July 27, police stormed the headquarters, setting off riots in the city in which at least five people died and scores of buildings and vehicles were set ablaze.

A strong government crackdown after the riots, which saw the worst violence in the city for over two decades, has since brought about a forced calm but analysts have said considerable dissatisfaction still prevails.

More than 200 people were taken into custody and several charged with subversion, a crime punishable by death. Megawati has not been detained but has been questioned three times by authorities in connection with the riots.
Mochtar Buchori, a columnist close to Megawati, said her campaign against the government would continue despite the pressure.
"Whether the movement is legal or extra-legal, it will still be a movement," he said. "She will still be in politics. She will still exist."
"This is the struggle of the people who have no real power. The struggle is symbolic but it is not really abstract. I think it is useful, but for the future," said Budiman.
Both added however that Megawati's focus appeared restricted to regaining the leadership of the PDI at its next congress in 1998.

In the meantime, dissent against the government appears to have no outlet, one Western diplomat said. "The pressure cooker seems to have been made a little bit tighter, and that's not a good thing," the diplomat said. "There's a general feeling of dissatisfaction that can ignite at any moment."
